mainTopic: Dew, wind and clouds that are never held back, mistakes in משיב הרוח ומוריד הגשם, and which weather helps the land
overview: The גמרא finishes explaining that ordinary טל (dew) is never held back. It explains that אליהו's oath was only about the special blessed dew. Next, רבי יהושע בן לוי proves from a פסוק in זכריה that wind never stops either. רבי חנינא then draws a practical הלכה for davening: mistakes about mentioning wind and dew never require repeating, but mistakes about rain do. A ברייתא says mentioning clouds and winds is optional because they are never held back. The גמרא answers a contradiction from רב יוסף by splitting clouds into early and late ones, and winds into ordinary and unusual ones. Finally, the גמרא discusses which weather after rain helps the land, citing עולא, רב יהודה and רבא. Snow on the mountains is worth five rainfalls, and רבא's list of what each kind of rain helps continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Dew is never held back
steps.stepSummary: The tail end of an earlier answer: the reason the פסוק did not mention dew is that dew is never withheld.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because dew is not withheld.
steps.whatsHappening: This line finishes an answer from just before. It explains why ה׳ promised to send rain but did not mention dew: dew never stops.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the גמרא noticed that when the drought in אליהו's time ended, the פסוק spoke only about rain. The answer is that dew had never stopped at all. This idea, that dew is always there, drives the rest of the section.

phrases.english: because it is not withheld.
phrases.notes: This finishes the answer from right before this: the פסוק promised rain but not dew, because dew never stops.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes an answer that began earlier on the daf
steps.terutzMaskana: Dew is constant, so it did not need to be promised back

steps.title: Why did אליהו swear about dew?
steps.stepSummary: If dew never stops, why did אליהו swear there would be no dew?
steps.simpleTranslation: And since dew is not withheld, why did אליהו need to swear that there would be no dew?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea from step 1. אליהו swore there would be no dew and no rain, but if dew can never stop, that oath makes no sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The principle that dew is never withheld seems to clash with a פסוק where אליהו says dew will stop. Either the principle is wrong, or the oath needs a different meaning.

phrases.english: And since it is not withheld,
why did Elijah need to swear?
phrases.notes: He means אליהו's oath that there would be no dew or rain: מלכים א 17:1.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the principle stated in step 1
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that dew is never withheld
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: אליהו swore dew would stop, which implies dew can be withheld

steps.title: Even the blessed dew will stop
steps.stepSummary: אליהו meant that even the special 'dew of blessing' would not come.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he said to him: even the dew of blessing will also not come.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that אליהו was not talking about ordinary dew. He meant the extra, helpful 'dew of blessing' would stop.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two kinds of dew: regular dew, which never stops, and טל של ברכה, which helps crops grow. אליהו's oath was about the second kind, so it does not contradict step 1.

keyTerms.meaning: Dew of blessing, the helpful dew that makes crops grow

phrases.english: This is what he said to him:
phrases.notes: אליהו is speaking to אחאב, the king.

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ טַל בְּרָכָה נָמֵי לָא אָתֵי.
phrases.english: Even the dew of blessing will also not come.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the term: a special kind of dew
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אליהו swore that all dew would stop
steps.terutzMaskana: He swore only about the blessed dew; ordinary dew continued

steps.title: Then why not bring back the blessed dew?
steps.stepSummary: If the blessed dew stopped, the פסוק should have promised to bring it back along with the rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then let Him bring back the dew of blessing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes further. If the blessed dew really stopped, then when the drought ended, the פסוק should have said ה׳ would return the blessed dew too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 3 fixed the oath but created a new problem. The פסוק that ends the drought mentions only rain, so where is the return of the blessed dew?

phrases.english: But let Him bring back the dew of blessing!
phrases.notes: He means in the פסוק where the drought ends, which mentions only rain: מלכים א 18:1.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 3
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the blessed dew had stopped
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If it stopped, its return should have been mentioned

steps.title: The difference cannot be noticed
steps.stepSummary: The return of the blessed dew was not mentioned because people cannot tell it apart from ordinary dew.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the matter is not noticeable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that there was no point in announcing the blessed dew's return. Nobody can see the difference between blessed dew and regular dew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rain coming back is obvious to everyone, so it was worth announcing. Blessed dew looks just like ordinary dew, which never stopped. So its return would not be something people could recognize.
steps.whatToRemember: Ordinary dew never stops. אליהו's oath was about the blessed dew, and its return was not mentioned because no one could see the difference.

phrases.english: Because the matter is not noticeable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 4 and closes the dew discussion
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical reasoning: the change cannot be seen
steps.terutzMaskana: Blessed dew's return is not announced because it cannot be told apart from ordinary dew

steps.title: How do we know wind never stops?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source that wind, like dew, is never held back.
steps.simpleTranslation: But winds, from where do we know that they are not withheld?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns from dew to wind. It asks how we know that wind never stops either.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea that wind is constant was assumed earlier together with dew. Now the גמרא wants a source for it, just as it had one for dew.

phrases.english: But winds, from where do we know
that they are not withheld?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from dew to wind
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source that wind is never withheld

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן לוי brings a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי quotes a פסוק in זכריה comparing ישראל to the four winds.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן לוי said: the פסוק says, 'For like the four winds of the heavens I have spread you out, says ה׳.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע בן לוי answers with a פסוק that compares ישראל to the four winds. How that proves wind never stops is explained in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At first it is not clear how this פסוק proves anything about wind. The גמרא will now ask what the פסוק means, and the proof will come from its exact wording.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי, דְּאָמַר קְרָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: because the verse says:
"For like the four winds of the heavens
I have spread you out, says the Lord."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי, דְּאָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 6
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק in זכריה about the four winds

steps.title: What is the פסוק telling ישראל?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the פסוק means and suggests a first reading: ה׳ scattered ישראל to the four directions.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is He saying to them? If you say that this is what הקדוש ברוך הוא is saying to ישראל: I scattered you to the four winds of the world...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the פסוק really means. It offers a simple first reading, that ישראל was scattered in every direction, and sets up a problem with it in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אילימא signals a suggestion that is about to be rejected. If the פסוק only means exile in all directions, it says nothing about wind never stopping.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (a suggestion about to be rejected)

phrases.english: What is He saying to them?
If you say this is what is said to them
by the Holy One, Blessed be He, to Israel:
that I scattered you to the four winds of the world,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how to read the פסוק brought in step 7
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the פסוק in זכריה

steps.title: The wording says 'like,' not 'to'
steps.stepSummary: If the פסוק meant scattering, it should say 'to the four winds,' not 'like the four winds.'
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why does it say 'like the four'? It should have said 'to the four'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the first reading because of one letter. The פסוק says כארבע (like the four), not בארבע (to the four).
steps.deeperAnalysis: Scattering people would be described as sending them 'to' the four directions. The word 'like' means ישראל is being compared to the winds, so the פסוק must be making a comparison.
steps.confusionAlert: Watch the letters: כְּ means 'like,' and בְּ means 'to' or 'in.' The whole proof depends on this one letter.

phrases.english: If so, why "like the four"?
It should have said "to the four"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggested reading of step 8
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the פסוק is about scattering
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The letter כ means comparison, not direction

steps.title: The world cannot exist without ישראל
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק means: just as the world cannot exist without winds, it cannot exist without ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what it says: just as the world cannot be without winds, so the world cannot be without ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the correct reading. ישראל is compared to the winds: the world always needs both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This comparison works only if winds are always present. So the פסוק teaches about ישראל and, along the way, proves that wind never stops, which answers step 6.
steps.whatToRemember: Wind never stops. We learn it from the פסוק that compares ישראל to the winds: the world cannot exist without either one.

phrases.english: Rather, this is what it says:

phrases.aramaic: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לָעוֹלָם בְּלֹא רוּחוֹת —
phrases.english: Just as it is impossible for the world to be without winds,

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ אִי אֶפְשָׁר לָעוֹלָם בְּלֹא יִשְׂרָאֵל.
phrases.english: so it is impossible for the world to be without Israel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected reading and completes the proof
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the פסוק as a comparison
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק describes scattering in four directions
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק compares ישראל to the ever-present winds, which proves wind never stops

steps.title: Mistakes in the summer
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא: in the summer, saying משיב הרוח by mistake is fine, but saying מוריד הגשם requires going back.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא said: therefore, in the summer, if one said 'He makes the wind blow,' we do not make him go back. If he said 'He makes the rain fall,' we make him go back.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא turns the idea into practical הלכה for davening. In the summer, mentioning wind is harmless, but mentioning rain is a real mistake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wind blows all year, so praising ה׳ for it in summer is still true. Rain in the summer is not a blessing, so mentioning it is a serious error and he must repeat.

keyTerms.meaning: We make him go back and repeat
'He makes the wind blow' (the praise in שמונה עשרה)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the practical הלכה about mistakes in משיב הרוח ומוריד הגשם in the second ברכה of שמונה עשרה.

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥanina said: Therefore,
in the summer:
if he said "He makes the wind blow,"
we do not make him go back.
phrases.notes: 'Go back' means he has to go back and say the ברכה again.

phrases.english: If he said "He makes the rain fall,"
we make him go back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a practical הלכה from the facts proven about טל and רוח
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In summer, mentioning wind does not require repeating; mentioning rain does

steps.title: Mistakes in the rainy season
steps.stepSummary: In the winter, leaving out wind is fine, but leaving out rain requires going back.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the rainy season: if he did not say 'He makes the wind blow,' we do not make him go back. If he did not say 'He makes the rain fall,' we make him go back.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא continues with the opposite season. In the winter, forgetting wind is no problem, but forgetting rain is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wind comes anyway, so leaving out its mention does not matter. Rain must be mentioned in its season, so leaving out מוריד הגשם means he must repeat.

phrases.english: In the rainy season:
if he did not say "He makes the wind blow,"
we do not make him go back.
If he did not say "He makes the rain fall,"
we make him go back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The winter half of רבי חנינא's ruling
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In winter, leaving out wind does not require repeating; leaving out rain does

steps.title: Even asking for wind and dew to stop is fine
steps.stepSummary: Even if he said the opposite, 'He removes the wind and makes the dew fly away,' he does not go back.
steps.simpleTranslation: And not only that, but even if he said 'He removes the wind and makes the dew fly away,' we do not make him go back.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא adds a bigger case. Even saying the opposite about wind and dew does not require repeating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since wind and dew never stop, his wrong words cannot affect anything. This is the strongest proof that mentions of wind and dew are not essential.

keyTerms.meaning: And not only that, but even

steps.whatToRemember: Because wind and dew are always there, mistakes about them in davening never require repeating. Mistakes about rain do require repeating.

phrases.english: And not only that, but
even if he said
"He removes the wind and makes the dew fly away,"
we do not make him go back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends רבי חנינא's ruling to an even stronger case
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even saying the opposite about wind and dew does not require repeating

steps.title: A ברייתא: no obligation to mention clouds and winds
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that חכמים did not require mentioning clouds or winds, but one may mention them if he wishes.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: חכמים did not require a person to mention clouds and winds. But if he wants to mention them, he may.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with the rule for clouds and winds. Mentioning them is allowed, but it is not required.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This builds on the earlier steps about טל and רוח. Here clouds and winds are put in a softer category. They are optional to mention, unlike rain (גשם), which must be mentioned.

phrases.english: It was taught:
With regard to clouds and winds,
the Sages did not require one to mention them,
but if he wants to mention them, he may mention them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a ברייתא that extends the rules about wind and dew to clouds and winds in general.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Mentioning clouds and winds is optional, not required.

steps.title: Why are clouds and winds optional?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the ברייתא's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why clouds and winds do not have to be mentioned. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It is a plain request for the reason. It is not an attack. The answer will set up the challenge that comes after it.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the ruling in step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why there is no obligation to mention clouds and winds.

steps.title: Because they are never held back
steps.stepSummary: Clouds and winds are optional to mention because they are never held back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because they are not held back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that clouds and winds always come, so there is no need to ask for them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rain can be held back as a punishment, so we must mention it. Clouds and winds always show up, so asking for them is not needed.

keyTerms.meaning: They are held back or stopped

phrases.english: Because they are not held back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Clouds and winds are never withheld, so there is no need to pray for them.

steps.title: רב יוסף's ברייתא says God does hold back clouds and winds
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף's ברייתא reads 'ועצר את השמים' as holding back clouds and winds, which contradicts the first ברייתא on both points.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are they really never held back? But רב יוסף taught: 'And He will close up the heavens' means from clouds and winds. You might think it only means rain. But the פסוק already says 'there will be no rain,' so rain is covered. So 'close up the heavens' must mean clouds and winds. This means the two ברייתות contradict each other about winds and about clouds!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reason it just gave. It brings a ברייתא that says God can hold back clouds and winds as a punishment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף shows that the פסוק already covers rain in its second half. So 'ועצר את השמים' must be teaching something extra: clouds and winds. That means they can be held back, which goes against 'דלא מיעצרי.' The גמרא then spells out two separate contradictions, one about winds and one about clouds.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't [he] teach? (introduces a contradicting source)
And He will close up the heavens
How do I fulfill (give meaning to) the words

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רב יוסף is arguing about davening. He is explaining a פסוק about punishment. The גמרא uses his reading to show that clouds and winds can be held back.

phrases.english: And are they not held back?
But didn't Rav Yosef teach:
"And He will close up the heavens"
means from the clouds and from the winds.

phrases.aramaic: אַתָּה אוֹמֵר מִן הֶעָבִים וּמִן הָרוּחוֹת,
phrases.english: You say from the clouds and from the winds,
or is it only from the rain?
When it says "so that there will be no rain,"
rain is already mentioned.

phrases.aramaic: הָא מָה אֲנִי מְקַיֵּים ״וְעָצַר אֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם״ —
phrases.english: So how do I give meaning to "And He will close up the heavens"?
It means from the clouds and from the winds.
So there is a contradiction between winds and winds,
and a contradiction between clouds and clouds!
phrases.notes: What the first ברייתא says about winds and clouds clashes with what רב יוסף says.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reason given in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that clouds and winds are never held back.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב יוסף's ברייתא reads the פסוק as God holding back clouds and winds, so they can be held back.

steps.title: Clouds: early ones versus late ones
steps.stepSummary: Early clouds before rain are never held back. Late clouds after rain can be held back.
steps.simpleTranslation: The clouds contradiction is not a problem. One ברייתא is about early clouds, and the other is about late clouds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the clouds contradiction by saying the two ברייתות are talking about different kinds of clouds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא is about early clouds that come before rain, and these always come. רב יוסף is talking about late clouds that come after rain. Those can be held back as a punishment.

phrases.english: Clouds against clouds is not difficult:
this one is about early clouds,
phrases.notes: The first ברייתא is talking about clouds that come before the rain.

phrases.english: and this one is about late clouds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the clouds half of the קשיא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (different kinds of clouds)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both ברייתות speak of the same clouds and contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Early clouds are never held back. Late clouds can be.

steps.title: Winds: ordinary versus unusual
steps.stepSummary: Ordinary winds are never held back. Unusual winds can be held back.
steps.simpleTranslation: The winds contradiction is not a problem. One ברייתא is about an ordinary wind, and the other is about an unusual wind.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the winds contradiction the same way, by splitting winds into two kinds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ordinary, everyday winds always blow, so we do not need to mention them. רב יוסף is talking about unusual, strong winds. Those can be held back.

phrases.english: Winds against winds is not difficult:
this one is about an ordinary wind,
and this one is about an unusual wind.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the winds half of the קשיא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (different kinds of winds)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both ברייתות speak of the same winds.
steps.terutzMaskana: Ordinary winds are never held back. Unusual winds can be.

steps.title: Isn't the unusual wind needed for threshing?
steps.stepSummary: An unusual wind is useful for winnowing grain, so we should have to pray for it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But an unusual wind is useful for the threshing floor!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer about winds. If unusual wind can be held back and people need it, why not require praying for it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Farmers used strong wind to separate grain from the husks. Since it can be held back and is needed, it seems it should be included in davening.

phrases.english: An unusual wind
is useful for the threshing floor!

steps.triggerLanguage: רוּחַ שֶׁאֵינָהּ מְצוּיָה חַזְיָא לְבֵי דָרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: Leaving the unusual wind out of the obligation to mention it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It is needed for threshing and can be held back, so it seems one should pray for it.

steps.title: Sieves can do the job
steps.stepSummary: Grain can be winnowed with sieves, so the unusual wind is not truly needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is possible to do it with sieves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that people can separate grain with sieves, so there is no real need to pray for unusual winds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We only require praying for things we cannot manage without. Since sieves work, the unusual wind is not essential. So the rule from step 14 stands.
steps.whatToRemember: Clouds and winds are optional to mention. Late clouds and unusual winds can be held back, but the unusual wind is not essential, because sieves can do its job.

phrases.english: It is possible to do it with sieves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the need is not essential
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The unusual wind is essential for threshing.
steps.terutzMaskana: Sieves can replace the wind, so there is no need to pray for it.

steps.title: Clouds and winds come right after rain in value
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that clouds and winds are second only to rain in how much they help.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: Clouds and winds are second to rain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that ranks clouds and winds just below rain in how useful they are.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier discussion was about which clouds and winds ה׳ might hold back. Now we hear a new, positive claim: clouds and winds are very valuable, almost as good as rain itself. The גמרא will next ask when this is true.

phrases.english: It was taught: The clouds and the winds
are second to rain.
phrases.notes: He means that in how much they help the land, they come right after rain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from which clouds and winds can be held back to a new teaching about how valuable they are.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Clouds and winds are second only to rain in their benefit.

steps.title: When is this true?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what kind of clouds and winds the ברייתא means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks in which situation clouds and winds are really that helpful. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Not every cloud or wind helps the land, so the ברייתא can't mean all of them. The גמרא wants to pin down exactly which ones it is talking about.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? (asking for the exact situation)

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the exact case behind the ברייתא in step 22.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which clouds and winds does the ברייתא say are second to rain?

steps.title: Clouds and winds that come after rain
steps.stepSummary: עולא (or רב יהודה) says the ברייתא means clouds and winds that come after the rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said, and some say רב יהודה: Those that come after rain.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer is given: the ברייתא is talking about clouds and winds that come after rain has fallen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Timing is the key. Clouds and winds right after rain help the ground, so those are the ones the ברייתא praises.

keyTerms.meaning: And some say (another version of who said it)

phrases.english: Ulla said, and some say Rav Yehuda:
Those that come after rain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא refers to clouds and winds that come after rainfall.

steps.title: But wind after rain is called a curse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: how can wind after rain be good, if the same teacher explained a curse in the תורה as wind after rain?
steps.simpleTranslation: Is this to say that it is a good thing? But it is written: 'ה׳ will make the rain of your land powder and dust,' and עולא, and some say רב יהודה, said: That is wind after rain!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the last answer. The same teacher also said that wind after rain is a curse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the curses of the תורה, rain turns into 'powder and dust,' and עולא (or רב יהודה) explained this as wind after rain that blows up dust. So wind after rain seems harmful, not helpful. The same person seems to be saying two opposite things.

keyTerms.meaning: Is this to say...? (opens a challenge)

phrases.english: Is this to say that it is beneficial?
But isn't it written: "The Lord will make the rain of your land
powder and dust",
and Ulla said, and some say Rav Yehuda:
This is wind that comes after rain!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer in step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that wind after rain is beneficial.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same teacher read the curse of 'powder and dust' as wind after rain, so wind after rain must be harmful.

steps.title: Gentle wind versus strong wind
steps.stepSummary: Gentle wind after rain helps; strong, forceful wind after rain is the curse.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult: This is when it comes gently, this is when it comes forcefully.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that there are two kinds of wind after rain, and the two statements talk about different kinds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A soft wind after rain is good, and that is what the ברייתא praises. A strong wind after rain is bad, and that is the curse in the פסוק. So both statements are true, just about different winds.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult (introduces an answer)

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is wind that comes gently,
that is wind that comes forcefully.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (two kinds of wind)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All wind after rain is the same, so it can't be both good and a curse.
steps.terutzMaskana: Gentle wind after rain is good; forceful wind after rain is the curse.

steps.title: Wind that raises dust versus wind that doesn't
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: wind after rain that raises dust is the curse; wind that doesn't raise dust is good.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: This is when it raises dust, this is when it does not raise dust.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers another way to split the two kinds of wind after rain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the dividing line is the dust, not the strength of the wind. This fits the wording of the curse, 'powder and dust.' Wind that leaves the dust alone is the helpful kind.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (introduces another answer)

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
this is wind that raises dust,
phrases.notes: Careful: the order flips from the last step. Here the first הָא is the harmful wind of the curse, and the second is the good wind.

phrases.english: that is wind that does not raise dust.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the challenge of step 25.
steps.terutzMaskana: Wind after rain that raises dust is the curse; wind that does not raise dust is beneficial.
steps.whatToRemember: Wind after rain can be good or bad. It is good when it is gentle (or doesn't raise dust), and bad when it is strong (or raises dust).

steps.title: Wind, clouds and sunshine after rain
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה: wind and clouds after rain are worth one rainfall, and sunshine after rain is worth two.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב יהודה said: Wind after rain is like rain. Clouds after rain are like rain. Sunshine after rain is like two rains.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה gives a new teaching that rates how helpful each kind of weather is after rain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This builds on the idea that what comes after rain can help. Wind and clouds each count as much as a rainfall. Sunshine counts double.

phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda said:
Wind after rain is like rain.
Clouds after rain are like rain.
Sunshine after rain is like two rainfalls.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A related teaching about weather after rain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wind and clouds after rain equal one rainfall; sunshine after rain equals two.

steps.title: What does this leave out?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what kind of weather after rain רב יהודה's list does not include.
steps.simpleTranslation: To exclude what?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what רב יהודה's list is meant to leave out. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If wind, clouds and sun after rain are all good, it sounds like everything after rain is good. The גמרא asks whether some weather after rain is not good.

keyTerms.meaning: To exclude what? (what is left out)

phrases.english: What does this come to exclude?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the limits of רב יהודה's statement in step 28.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which weather after rain is not beneficial?

steps.title: Evening glow and patchy sun are not good
steps.stepSummary: The list leaves out the evening glow and sun peeking between clouds; these are not good after rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: To exclude the glow of the night, and sun between the clouds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: two kinds of light after rain are left out, the evening glow and sun shining through gaps in the clouds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only full sunshine after rain is worth two rainfalls. A glow at night or sun breaking through in patches does not count, because these are not good after rain.

keyTerms.meaning: The glow of the night (evening light)

phrases.english: To exclude the glow of the night,
and sun that shines between the clouds.
phrases.notes: קַרְחֵי literally means bald spots, the open gaps between clouds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 29.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Evening glow and patchy sunshine after rain are excluded; they are not beneficial.

steps.title: Snow on mountains is worth five rainfalls
steps.stepSummary: רבא teaches that snow on the mountains helps as much as five rainfalls on the land, based on a פסוק in איוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Snow is good for the mountains like five rainfalls for the land, as it says: 'For He says to the snow: Fall on the earth, and the shower of rain, and the showers of His mighty rain.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds a related teaching: snow on the mountains is very helpful, and he brings a פסוק to prove it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק lists snow together with several words for rain. רבא counts the rain words as five, so snow is worth five rainfalls.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is said (brings a פסוק)

steps.whatToRemember: After rain, gentle wind, clouds and full sunshine help the land, but patchy sun and evening glow do not. Snow on the mountains is worth five rainfalls.

phrases.english: Rava said: Snow is beneficial for the mountains
like five rainfalls for the land,
as it is stated: "For He says to the snow: Fall on the earth,
and the shower of rain, and the showers of His mighty rain."
phrases.notes: Count the rain words: גֶּשֶׁם twice, מָטָר once, and מִטְרוֹת, which is plural so it counts as two. That makes five.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, related teaching about how helpful different weather is.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Snow on the mountains is as beneficial as five rainfalls on the land.

steps.title: רבא matches each kind of rain to what it helps
steps.stepSummary: רבא teaches that snow benefits the mountains, strong rain benefits trees, and light rain benefits fruit.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא said: Snow is good for the mountains. Strong rain is good for the trees. Gentle rain is good for the fruit.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a second teaching on the same topic as his last one, listing which kind of precipitation helps which part of the land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the last step רבא said snow on the mountains is worth five rainfalls. Now he widens the picture: each type of precipitation has its own target, with snow for mountains, strong rain for trees and gentle rain for fruit.

phrases.english: And Rava said:
Snow is good for the mountains;
strong rain is good for the trees;
light rain is good for the fruit;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching by רבא that expands on his statement about snow in step 31, now covering several kinds of precipitation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each kind of precipitation has its own benefit: snow for mountains, strong rain for trees, light rain for fruit.
